  PRESENTATIONS

  1. Traffic Safety Review of Main Street between Westmont Drive to Hampden Terrace

  Staff will review the report that was prepared in response to a concern of motorists having difficulty
  exiting from Westmont Drive onto northbound Main Street and the speed of traffic as cars curve
  onto Main Street east towards Hampden Terrace.

  After a thorough review of existing field conditions, speed data and average daily traffic, it was
  determined that traffic calming measures be installed along W. Main Street between Westmont
  Drive and Hampden Terrace to reduce the speed of vehicles as they enter W. Main Street.

  Recommended Action

  It is recommended that the Transportation Commission review the report with the City Traffic
  Engineer, listen to public comment and authorize staff to implement the additional safety
  measures outlined in the report.

  2. Traffic Safety Review Poplar Boulevard between Fremont Avenue and the city of
  Alhambra’s West city limit

  Staff will review the report that was prepared in response to a citizen request to assess existing
  conditions along the segment of Poplar Boulevard between Fremont Avenue and the city of
  Alhambra’s west city limit.

  The study finds that the City has the appropriate traffic calming measures currently in place for
  the study segment of Poplar Boulevard between Winchester Avenue and Fremont Avenue.

  Recommended Action

  It is recommended that the Transportation Commission review the report with the City Traffic
  Engineer, listen to public comment and authorize staff to implement the additional safety
  measures outlined in the report.

 3. Traffic Safety Review of Montezuma Avenue between Fremont Avenue and Palm
  Avenue

Staff will review the report that was prepared in response to a citizen request for a stop sign with
Stop bar on Date Avenue at Montezuma Avenue as well as on Primrose Avenue at Montezuma
Avenue.

The study recommends the installation of a Stop sign and Stop bar at Primrose Avenue and Date
Avenue as they intersect with Montezuma Avenue. Both of these locations are along the route to
the Granada Park with sidewalks on both sides of Montezuma Avenue so vehicles exiting along
these side streets may encounter pedestrians.

Recommended Action

It is recommended that the Transportation Commission review the report with the City Traffic
Engineer, listen to public comment and authorize staff to implement the additional safety
measures outlined in the report.

communications to five (5) minutes.

Comments, concerns or discussion on any item(s) not specified on the agenda. Items discussed
must pertain to the business of the Alhambra Transportation Commission.

  Adjournment to a regular meeting on Wednesday, May 12, 2021 at 7:00 p.m.

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND

On behalf of the City of Alhambra, Transtech Engineers Inc. has completed a traffic review to evaluate the
traffic conditions along Main Street between Westmont Drive to Hampden Terrace. The City has received
a concern of motorists having difficulty exiting from Westmont Drive onto northbound Main Street and
the speed of traffic as cars curve onto Main Street east towards Hampden Terrace. As part of the traffic
review the following items were looked at: a review of the existing roadway conditions, 6 years of collision
history, peak hour and daily traffic counts and a 24-hour radar speed sample.

W. Main Street - Within the City of Alhambra, W. Main Street runs east/west and is considered a major
arterial road per the City’s General Plan with two different posted speed limits. North/West from the
intersection of W. Main Street/Huntington Drive and Westmont Drive, the posted speed limit is 35 mph.

After Main Street splits with Huntington Drive EB the posted speed limit is 30 mph. The segment of W.
Main Street from Westmont Drive to Hampden Terrace is essentially a one-way street with traffic traveling
northeast. After the split, heading east toward Hampden Terrace, W. Main Street is approximately 40-
feet wide and consists of two travel lanes with parking available on both sides of the street except along
red curbed areas. Land use along this section is Commercial Planned Development zoning.

Westmont Drive - Within the City of Alhambra, Westmont Drive runs north/south and is considered a
local road per the City’s General Plan with a prima facie speed limit of 25 MPH. At the intersection of
Westmont Drive at W. Main Street, Westmont Drive is approximately 32-feet wide with one lane in each
direction and no marked centerline separating opposing traffic. Northbound travel along Westmont Drive
is restricted to right turns only onto W. Main Street since there is a center median preventing vehicles
from turning left onto W. Main Street. Parking along Westmont Drive is allowed on both sides of
Westmont Drive except on the east side of Westmont Drive on Thursdays from 8am-11:30am due to street
sweeping. Parking is also not allowed on the west side of Westmont Drive on Thursdays from Noon – 3pm.
Westmont Drive primarily runs through a single-family residential area at the south end and Commercial
Planned Development at the north end.

Hampden Terrace - Within the City of Alhambra, Hampden Terrace runs north/south and is considered a
local road per the City’s General Plan with a prima facie speed limit of 25 MPH. At the intersection of
Hampden Terrace at W. Main Street, Hampden Terrace is approximately 28-feet wide with one lane in
each direction and approximately 45-feet of a marked solid yellow centerline. Northbound travel along
Hampden Terrace at W. Main Street restricts vehicles from traveling straight past W. Main Street due to
existing right turn only pavement markings. Southbound travel along Hampden Terrace at W. Main Street
allows vehicles to proceed straight or turn left onto W. Main Street. Hampden Terrace primarily runs
through a single-family residential area at the south end and Commercial Planned Development at the
north end.

CRITERIA FOR DETERMINING IF ALL-WAY STOP CONTROL IS WARRANTED

As part of this report a review of the requirements for installing All-Way Stop was included. The resident
complaint to the City included the request for the installation of ALL-Way Stop at the intersection of
Westmont Drive and Main Street. Traffic control devices work in concert with the basic “rules of the road”
contained in traffic laws and ordinances. The California Manual of Uniform Traffic Devices (CAMUTCD
Section 2B.07) describes applications and warrants that guide the placement of STOP signs (R1-1). The
STOP sign is a regulatory device that is used when traffic is required to stop. STOP signs are used to assign
right-of-way at an intersection. Multi-way stop control is used where the volume of traffic on the
intersecting roads is approximately equal.

Stop signs are not used as a speed control device. Since a STOP sign causes inconvenience to motorists, it
should be used only where warranted. The placement of these signs is dictated by engineering judgment
and based on guidelines found in the CAMUTCD and CVC. The City’s criteria for determining if two-way
or all-way stop control is warranted is based on a number of factors as set by the CAMUTCD. These factors
include minimum volume on each of the street approaches, accident investigation, speed of traffic,
number of pedestrians and potential sight obstructions.

All-Way Stop Installation

The following briefly outlines the Criteria for the installation of All-Way stop warrants as found in Section
2B.07 of the CAMUTCD.

ALL-WAY STOP CONTROL WARRANTS FOR INSTALLATION

The placement of All-Way stop control is warranted when:
  A. Traffic control signals are justified
  B. A crash problem exists as indicated by 5 or more accidents in a 12-month period
  C. Minimum Volumes are met if,:
  1. Volume entering intersection from the major approach (total of both approaches)
  averages 300 vehicles per hour for any 8 hours of an average day.
  2. The combined vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle volumes entering the intersection from the
  minor street approaches averages at least 200 units per hour for the same 8 hours.
  3. If the 85th percentile approach speed of the major street exceeds 40 MPH, the minimum
  volumes are 70 percent of the above values.

As a part of this study, a review of the intersection of W. Main Street and Westmont Drive was conducted.
Based on the analysis and field review conducted it was determined that the intersections did not meet
the warrants for the installation of All-Way STOP control. Main Street carries a significant amount of
traffic compared to Westmont Drive. This unbalanced volume in the streets would potentially cause a
back up in traffic on Main Street as well as the increase in running a STOP sign that motorists feel is not
needed.

the intersecting highway to permit the driver to
anticipate and avoid potential collisions (Maze and
Plazak 2000). These unobstructed views form
triangular areas are known as sight triangles as seen
  Figure 6: Example of Stopping Sight Distance Triangle
in Figure 6. Any object within the sight triangle that
would obstruct the driver’s view of an approaching vehicle should be removed or modified or appropriate

TRAFFIC CALMING DEVICES AND STRATEGIES

Traffic calming is the process of reducing vehicle speeds through the use of both passive devices, such as
signs and striping, and physical devices such as changes in road elevation or path. As part of this study,
traffic speeds, accidents and traffic volumes were used to assess existing conditions along this segment.
The type, design and placement of traffic calming devices depend upon the road classification, desired
traffic speed and types of traffic issues along W. Main Street.

A single traffic calming device placed along a long stretch of road will be marginally effective at slowing
down speed at that isolated location. Implementation of a series of traffic calming devices that work
together will effectively slow down traffic speeds along the length of the corridor. There are various traffic
calming measures that can reduce the flow and speed of traffic on a street. Some of these are:

1) Traffic Education Campaign: This consists of flyers, neighborhood meetings, banners and other
  notices to assist is making the public aware of the traffic conditions in a certain area. The goal is to
  educate residents and non-residents about basic traffic laws, speed limits and safety conditions near
  schools.

  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
  Prepared By: Transtech Engineers, Inc. | Page 8 of 18
   TRAFFIC REVIEW OF MAIN STREET FROM WESTMONT DR TO HAMPDEN TERRACE

2) Signage and Pavement Legends: Modifying the signage along the road or change the striping to
  narrow travel lanes effectively slow speeds by changing the travel environment. Signs alert the Driver
  to their speed, such as larger speed limit signs or a speed feedback sign. Too many signs can have an
  opposite effect on traffic. Therefore, usage of signs should be subject to careful consideration and
  compliance with local and regional standards. Speed and stop ahead legends alert the drivers of a
  change in traffic conditions. Speed limit signs and striped speed limit pavement “messages,” either
  used separately or as a combination, are one of the most cost effective measures in increasing
  awareness of motorists traveling through a neighborhood street. These two devices do not have
  glaring negative impacts as far as air quality, emergency response time, maintenance, and liability
  exposure.

3) Larger Dimension Signs: Installation of larger dimensioned signage are recommended as treatments
  to increase the motorist’s awareness and other Driver conditions by highlighting various areas of the
  roadway. All sign dimensions should comply with the dimensions specified in the California Manual of
  Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CAMUTCD) Table 2B-1 Regulatory Sign and Plaque Sizes. The sizes
  are shown in the multi-lane column as 36” x 36” for stop signs and 30” x 36” for speed limits.

4) Traffic Striping: Roadway striping can be implemented as an option that is a low cost alternative to
  vertical/horizontal traffic calming measures. This includes a white stripe painted along both sides of
  the travel way to give the driver a perception of a narrower road. Changing the striping to narrow
  travel lanes effectively slows speeds by changing the travel environment. Narrower lanes create
  “friction” and thereby cause Drivers to travel at a slower pace. This has been used in Alhambra as well
  as other local cities such as in West Covina, Rosemead, Temple City, Newport Beach, San Clemente,
  and Irvine. This traffic calming measure is considered to be less costly with minor impacts to
  neighborhoods.

  These have:
  • Less impacts to emergency services
  • Less costly
  • Greater flexibility (can be installed or removed easily)
  • No impact to drainage
  • Can provide parking lanes
  • Found to reduce speeds from 1 mph to 7 mph

  Traffic striping as a traffic calming device can effectively reduce speed on a roadway. This is
  particularly effective on long, straight roadways where there are wide travel lanes for long distances.
  Striping has shown to reduce speed effectively as a first step in the traffic calming process, as
  documented in surveys and traffic calming sources 1.

5) Radar Feedback Signs: Radar feedback signs are an effective way
  to alert Drivers of their speed. A portable sign surveys the speed
  of each passing vehicle and displays the speed information on a
  board next to the posted speed limit. The sign is used as passive
  enforcement to inform Drivers of their travel speed. There would
  also be an initial cost to purchase the units.

6) Targeted Police Enforcement: The police department deploys
  officers to perform enforcement on residential streets for at least
  an hour a day. The goal is to make Drivers aware of the speed
  limits and reduce speeds. This requires the cooperation and
  dedication of police enforcement. This has been shown to be a
  good spot enforcement technique.

RECOMMENDATIONS

After a thorough review of existing field conditions, speed data and average daily traffic, it was determined
that traffic calming measures be installed along W. Main Street between Westmont Drive and Hampden
Terrace to reduce the speed of vehicles as they enter W. Main Street. Please refer to Figure 7 for an aerial
demonstration of the proposed conditions and see Figures 8 thru Figure 11 for a Street View of the
proposed conditions:

Recommendations

1. Install 15-feet of red curb beginning at the corner of Westmont Drive and W. Main Street to the
  west/south first driveway on W. Main Street. CVC 21458.
  • This will improve the line of sight for drivers exiting the intersection of Westmont Drive onto Main
  Street. Figure 8

2. Install Side Stripes along the south side of W. Main Street, approximately 8-feet from the curb
  between Westmont Drive to Hampden Terrace. Install side stripe as a continuation of the white

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND

The City of Alhambra received a resident request to assess existing conditions along the segment of Poplar
Boulevard between Fremont Avenue and the city of Alhambra’s west city limit. According to the resident,
vehicles are speeding along Poplar Boulevard, as well as ignoring the flashing stop signs posted on the
street. The residents also noted that noise laws are being violated by loud vehicles, as well as five axle
trucks over 15,000 pounds violating their prohibition on this street.

The resident stated that there have been several collisions along the segment due to these violations and
is specifically asking for speed bumps along Poplar Boulevard, adding that Poplar Boulevard is a residential
road and has a school where children frequently travel. As part of the traffic review the following items
were reviewed: existing roadway conditions, 5 years of collision history, new daily traffic counts including
a 24-hour count by axle, and output from a 24-hour radar speed sample.

TRAFFIC CALMING DEVICES AND STRATEGIES

Traffic calming is the process of reducing vehicle speeds through the use of both passive devices, such as
signs and striping, and physical devices such as changes in road elevation or path. As part of this study,
traffic speeds, accidents and traffic volumes were used to assess existing conditions along this segment.
The type, design and placement of traffic calming devices depend upon the road classification, desired
traffic speed and types of traffic issues along Poplar Avenue. The following is a list of common traffic
calming measures usually deployed to reduce speeding, increase visibility of signs, decrease running of
Stop signs. As shown in Figure 2 most of the typical traffic calming measures have been installed along
Poplar Avenue. This includes additional signage and pavement legends, beacons on Stop Signs, speed
limit signs and radar speed feedback signs as well as side stripes to visually narrow the travel lanes.

2)  Signage and Pavement Legends
3)  Larger Dimension Signs or Beacons on Signs

TRAFFIC CIRCLE

As part of this review the resident asked that the City explore the possibility of installing a Traffic Circle or
Roundabout at the ALL-Way Stop controlled “T” intersection of Poplar Boulevard and Orange Grove
Avenue. A mini roundabout or traffic circle is a circular raised or painted center island where drivers travel
counterclockwise. There are no traffic signals or stop signs in a modern roundabout. Drivers yield at entry
to traffic in the roundabout, then enter the intersection and exit essentially making right turns.

The main advantage of traffic circles is that they reduce the number of conflict points for vehicles.
However, to be effective the traffic circle needs to have a large enough diameter or roadway width for
the circle to be large enough to force vehicles to slow down to make an actual right turn around the circle.
The travel way around the circle would need to provide a travel path that motorists would not run over
the traffic circle and is large enough to provide for gaps in circling traffic to allow for vehicles to enter from
lesser side streets. The design of all traffic circles or mini roundabouts needs to follow CAMUTCD
guidelines. A mini roundabout on a residential street is intended to keep speeds to a minimum. LA County
Guidelines for the Design of Roundabouts requires a roadway width of 60’ feet to accommodate the
splitter islands for approach traffic.

RECOMMENDATIONS

As a result of extensive field data collection and review of existing traffic conditions it is determined that
the City of Alhambra has the appropriate traffic calming measures currently in place for the study segment
of Poplar Boulevard between Winchester Avenue and Fremont Avenue. The data obtained does not
support additional traffic calming measures at this time. The roadway is not wide enough (60’) to provide
the necessary circle diameter to effectively slow traffic without causing undue delay to emergency
vehicles or impacts to on-street parking for those residents within the splitter island for the approach to
a roundabout. A roundabout is not recommended along Poplar Boulevard. At this stage the following
measures should be undertaken:

  1.  Service the existing Solar powered Flashing LED Stop (R1-1) Sign for west bound travel along
  Poplar Boulevard at Westmont Drive to ensure that it is functioning properly.
  2.  Notify Alhambra PD to provide spot speed enforcement and to give citations for any large
  trucks using Poplar Boulevard as a cut thru route.

CRITERIA FOR STOP CONTROL INSTALLATION

The installation of traffic control devices on public streets are guided by the California Manual on Uniform
Traffic Control Devices (CAMUTCD), the California Vehicle Code (CVC) and engineering judgement. The

 TRAFFIC REVIEW OF MINOR STREET STOP SIGN REQUEST ALONG PRIMROSE AVENUE AND DATE AVENUE ENTERING MONTEZUMA AVENUE

CAMUTCD provides guidelines along with engineering judgement where installation of a STOP sign on a
minor street approach can be installed. Traffic control devices work in concert with the basic “rules of the
road” contained in traffic laws and ordinances. CVC sections 21354 and 21355 allows local authorities to
erect STOP signs at any location so as to control traffic at an intersection.

As guidance, the CAMUTCD states that YIELD or STOP signs could be used at an intersection if one or more
of the following conditions exist:

  A. An intersection of a less important road with a main road where application of the normal right-
  of-way rule would not be expected to provide reasonable compliance with the law;
  B. A street entering a designated through highway or street; and/or
  C. An unsignalized intersection in a signalized area.

Along with engineering judgement the CAMUTCD has provided further guidance in the placement of STOP
signs.

Section 2B.06 STOP Sign Guidance

  1.  At intersections where a full stop is not necessary at all times, consideration should first be given
  to using less restrictive measures such as YIELD signs (see Sections 2B.08 and 2B.09).
  2. The use of STOP signs on the minor-street approaches should be considered if engineering
  judgment indicates that a stop is always required because of one or more of the following
  conditions:
  3. The vehicular traffic volumes on the through street or highway exceed 6,000 vehicles per day;
  A restricted view exists that requires road users to stop in order to adequately observe conflicting
  traffic on the through street or highway; and/or
  4. Crash records indicate that three or more crashes that are susceptible to correction by the
  installation of a STOP sign have been reported within a 12-month period, or that five or more
  such crashes have been reported within a 2-year period. Such crashes include right-angle
  collisions involving road users on the minor-street approach failing to yield the right-of-way to
  traffic on the through street or highway.

RECOMMENDATIONS

It is recommended to install a Stop sign and Stop bar at Primrose Avenue and Date Avenue as they
intersect with Montezuma Avenue. Both of these locations are along the route to the Granada Park with
sidewalks on both sides of Montezuma Avenue so vehicles exiting along these side streets may encounter
pedestrians. Since schools are not in session and park usage is limited good average daily counts were
unable to be conducted on Montezuma Avenue. Montezuma Avenue has a posted speed of 25 mph but
is used as a route to the park as well as access to Palm Avenue that gets to Hellman Avenue over to Atlantic
Blvd so a STOP would force vehicles on the side streets to make a STOP before merging onto Montezuma
Avenue.

Posting of STOP signs on the minor street only will ensure vehicles are slowing down and coming to a
complete stop before exiting onto Montezuma Avenue. This will also improve motorist, pedestrian, and
bicyclist safety.
